summary:
Puerto Rico is a United States territory, and the United States federal framework applies on the island in full: federal statutes, executive orders and agency procedure govern entry, documents, federally funded care and federal custody. Puerto Rico's own legislation does not soften that framework, and in the area of trans medical care it sharpens it.

United States travel documents record sex assigned at birth, and Executive Order 14168, signed 20 January 2025, eliminated the X marker, so a trans visitor arriving on United States documents may present a marker that does not match their appearance at inspection. Entry scrutiny is tightened further for one category of traveller: in February 2025 the United States State Department announced visa denials for trans athletes seeking entry to compete in women's sports.

Consensual private sexual activity between adults is not criminalised in Puerto Rico. The Puerto Rico Supreme Court upheld the territory's sodomy ban in 2002; the United States Supreme Court's Lawrence v. Texas ruling in 2003 invalidated state and territorial sodomy statutes covering consensual private acts, and Puerto Rico amended its Penal Code in 2004 to remove private, non-commercial sexual activity between consenting adults from the statute.

In July 2025 Puerto Rico banned gender-affirming care for anyone under 21, barred public funding for that care, and set penalties of up to 15 years in prison, a $50,000 fine and permanent loss of medical licences for doctors who violate the ban. The Puerto Rico LGBTQ+ Federation announced plans to challenge the ban in court.

The care law was pushed through non-public hearings and is written with deliberate vagueness, so doctors and affirming parents who facilitate hormone treatment or top surgery risk prosecution. It mandates campaigns by the Education and Health departments on the risks of trans-affirming care. Health Secretary Ramos Otero proposed amendments that would have allowed puberty blockers and the continuation of existing hormone treatment, but the text as enacted stands as the most restrictive care law in any United States jurisdiction according to the report documenting it. For a trans visitor the ban closes off gender-affirming care on the island for anyone under 21, and the facilitation language reaches the accompanying parents of a travelling trans teenager.

No prohibition on conversion therapy for minors is in force. Senate Bill 1000, which would have banned the practice for minors, cleared the Senate with governor support but was blocked from a floor vote in the House in March 2019 by the pro-statehood NPP caucus, with co-sponsor Senator Zoe Laboy dissenting publicly. In April 2019 Governor Rossello announced Senate Bills 1253 and 1254, the second carrying a pastoral exemption for clergy; LGBT council president Johanne Velez Garcia and allies said the pairing would open doors to refusal of service on orientation and gender-identity grounds, and the governor asked lawmakers to withdraw both bills on 13 June 2019.

Puerto Rico amended its hate crime statutes in 2002 to include sexual orientation and gender identity as protected characteristics, and the territory is also covered by the United States federal Matthew Shepard and James Byrd, Jr. Hate Crimes Prevention Act. The first hate crime charges in Puerto Rico's history were brought in 2020, after Sean Díaz de León and Juan Pagán Bonilla were charged in the murder of two transgender women on 22 April 2020; Bonilla confessed to the killings. In January 2021 Governor Pedro Pierluisi declared a state of emergency over ongoing murders, assaults and rape of transgender individuals on the island.

Anti-discrimination coverage remains partial. The 2013 law that passed (Senate Bill 238, signed 29 May 2013) was amended in the House to apply only to employment discrimination, so public facilities, housing, transit and business transactions are not covered by it. An earlier bill, House Bill 1725, passed the House 43-6 in November 2009 with wider coverage but the Senate held no hearings and took no action after Senate President Thomas Rivera Schatz said it would not be approved.

Marriage recognition for same-sex couples in Puerto Rico was won through federal court rather than local statute. The challenge filed in March 2014, the Ada Conde Vidal case, drew intervention from Lambda Legal and Puerto Rico Para Todas, and in June 2014 four couples joined as plaintiffs, among them a former National Guard member and two couples already married in Canada in 2007 and New York in 2012.

Under Executive Order 14168, which directs United States federal agencies to recognise only two sexes, the Bureau of Prisons houses transgender inmates by sex assigned at birth rather than asserted gender identity, a rule that governs any federal custody in Puerto Rico. The ACLU said it had received reports that transgender women were being transferred to men's prisons, told they would be, or moved to solitary confinement, and the Bureau of Prisons stopped reporting how many transgender people it holds. Advocates say the order contravenes the Prison Rape Elimination Act requirement that trans inmates' housing be decided by individual safety assessment.
tangentialFactors:
Puerto Rico's care statute is described by the report documenting it as the most restrictive gender-affirming care law in any United States jurisdiction, which places the territory ahead of the national trend rather than merely following it.

Religious-freedom legislation has twice been turned back. Governor Ricardo Rosselló vetoed a 2017 bill that would have let public businesses refuse service to LGBTQ people in February 2018, and withdrew a similar 2019 pairing on 13 June 2019 after House approval amid protests. The pattern indicates that organised local opposition has stopped carve-outs permitting refusal of service on gender-identity grounds, while the underlying statutory gaps in the employment-only 2013 law remain unremedied.

The territory's hate-crime machinery exists on paper and has been used once: the 2020 charges over the killings of two transgender women were the first hate crime charges in Puerto Rico's history, and the January 2021 state of emergency was declared against a background of continuing murders, assaults and rape of transgender people.

Federal and local layers can point in opposite directions for a visitor. Federal documents and custody rules are fixed by Executive Order 14168, while local statutes add the under-21 care ban and its criminal penalties on top of that framework.
localsOnly:
House Bill 488, signed 29 May 2013, extended domestic violence protections to all households regardless of sexual orientation and gender identity, so residents have a route to protection from intimate-partner violence that does not depend on the employment-only 2013 anti-discrimination law.

Residents have no statutory ban on conversion therapy for minors: Senate Bill 1000 died in the House in March 2019 despite Senate passage and governor support, and the replacement pairing of Senate Bills 1253 and 1254, which carried a pastoral exemption for clergy, was withdrawn on 13 June 2019 after sustained opposition from LGBT advocates and the LGBT council.

Discrimination in housing, public facilities, transit and business transactions falls outside Senate Bill 238 as enacted, and the wider House Bill 1725 never received Senate consideration after Senate President Thomas Rivera Schatz said it would not be approved.

Doctors and parents who facilitate hormone treatment or top surgery face prosecution under the July 2025 care law, with penalties of up to 15 years in prison, a $50,000 fine and permanent loss of medical licences, and the Puerto Rico LGBTQ+ Federation has announced a court challenge to the statute.
outOfScopeNotes:
No separate Puerto Rico Department of Corrections policy on transgender inmate housing, no dedicated unit and no judicial ruling on the question were located in the sources, so the treatment of a trans person held in territorial rather than federal custody on the island is unresolved.

Whether the July 2025 care law's facilitation language has been applied to a parent accompanying a travelling trans teenager, or to a visitor under 21 seeking care, is not documented in the sources; the risk stated here follows from the statute's text and its reported vagueness, not from a reported prosecution.

The sources do not state how the elimination of the X marker under Executive Order 14168 affects United States passports already issued with that marker, or what inspection officers do when a document marker conflicts with presentation.

Enforcement of the 2002 hate crime amendments beyond the 2020 prosecutions, and the current status of the January 2021 state of emergency, are not sourced here.
